589.title: Rejoice always (Philippians 4:4–7)
589.hook: be nothing solicitous, and the peace of God keeps your hearts
589.howItsDone: On the Third Sunday of Advent, Gaudete Sunday, Catholics light the rose candle on the Advent wreath, priests may wear rose vestments, and the entrance antiphon is taken from Philippians 4:4–5.

segments.voice: Yesterday, forgetting what's behind: the past no longer steers, and the runner strains forward. Your line was press on.

On one Sunday in Advent, a Catholic priest may set aside the purple and wear rose. On the wreath, the pink candle is lit. That Sunday has a name, Gaudete, the Latin for rejoice, from the first word of the old entrance chant. And the chant is today's verse: Gaudete in Domino semper, rejoice in the Lord always. The surprising part is where Paul was when he wrote it. Not on a holiday. In prison, not knowing whether he'd live or die.
screen: `ROSE VESTMENTS IN ADVENT.` → `GAUDETE: REJOICE.` → `WRITTEN FROM PRISON.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice. Let your modesty be known to all men. The Lord is nigh." He says it twice, as if he expects them to hesitate. Modesty here translates a Greek word that means something like gentleness or graciousness, not grabbing what's yours. Then: the Lord is nigh. Near. Near in time, coming soon? Or near in space, right beside you? Readers have taken it both ways, and the verse can hold both. Then comes the instruction: "Be nothing solicitous; but in every thing, by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your petitions be made known to God." Be nothing solicitous is an old way of saying don't be anxious about anything. And notice what Paul doesn't say. He doesn't say stop worrying because there's nothing to worry about. He says take the worry and turn it into a request, with thanks attached. Then the promise: "And the peace of God, which surpasseth all understanding, keep your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus." The Greek for keep is a soldier's word: to guard, to garrison. Acts calls Philippi a colony: a piece of Rome set down in Macedonia. Paul pictures God's peace standing guard at the gate of your heart. Not peace that understands everything. Peace that surpasses understanding: in Paul's words, it can hold even when the situation doesn't make sense. On Gaudete Sunday, the Church is still waiting for Christmas. The rejoicing comes before the gifts are open.

segments.voice: Let the loudest worry of the day come to the front, and name it plainly. Instead of chewing on it, shape it into a request, help with this, watch over them, show me the next step, and set one thing you're thankful for right next to it. If you pray, make it known to God just as it is; if not, set it down in words and notice whether anything loosens.
Rejoice always. Paul's words from prison, sung every Gaudete Sunday: rejoice in the Lord always, for the Lord is nigh. Today's word.
Your line: the lord is nigh. Near in time, and near beside you. Until tomorrow.

590.title: Whatsoever things are true (Philippians 4:8)
590.hook: think on whatever is true, modest, just, holy, lovely
590.howItsDone: Catholic spiritual writers encourage guarding the imagination and filling the mind with good things through spiritual reading, sacred art and music; Philippians 4:8 is often quoted in that advice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rejoice always: a worry turned into a request, and peace standing guard. Your line was the lord is nigh.

Scroll back through what you looked at yesterday. Not to judge it. Just to notice what filled your head. The headlines. The arguments. The videos. The things you checked three times. Whatever gets in, stays a while and moves the furniture around. Paul seems to have known this long before screens. Near the end of his letter to Philippi, after rejoicing and peace, he gives his friends a list. Not of things to do. Of things to think about.
screen: `WHAT FILLED YOUR HEAD YESTERDAY?` → `WHAT GETS IN, STAYS.` → `A LIST OF THINGS TO THINK ABOUT.`

segments.voice: "For the rest, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever modest, whatsoever just, whatsoever holy, whatsoever lovely, whatsoever of good fame, if there be any virtue, if any praise of discipline, think on these things." Eight items. Some are familiar church words: just, holy. But others sound less like church and more like the Greek philosophers' schools. Virtue, aretē, was one of their great words: excellence. Lovely means lovable, winning, the kind of thing people are drawn to. Of good fame means well spoken of. Paul is reaching into the best of the wider culture and saying: that too. Whatever is true, wherever you find it. Then the verb: think on these things. The Greek word is logizesthe, a counting word, used for reckoning accounts. Take stock of these. Add them up. Dwell on them on purpose. Christian thinkers took this openness seriously. Justin Martyr wrote that whatever had been rightly said by anyone belongs to Christians. Centuries later, Thomas Aquinas read Aristotle with great care. And Paul ties the list to a promise in the next verse: do the things you've learned and seen, and the God of peace will be with you. This isn't about ignoring the hard news. Paul is in prison while he writes it. It's about choosing what you let settle in the mind, and what you leave at the door.

If you pray, thank God for it; if not, let it stay and take up room.

591.title: Content (Philippians 4:11–13)
591.hook: I have learned to be content, and I can do all things in him
591.howItsDone: Catholic teaching on the tenth commandment commends "poverty of heart" and freedom from envy and greed; Catholics practice contentment through simplicity, fasting and almsgiving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, arete: whatever is true, whatever lovely, think on these things. Your line was think on these.

I can do all things. It turns up on gym shirts, on locker-room walls, under an athlete's eyes in black grease paint. There it reads like a promise of winning: with God's help I'll make the team, close the deal, run the marathon. Read in place, it's something quieter. It comes near the end of a thank-you note. The church at Philippi had sent Paul a gift in prison, carried by a friend named Epaphroditus. And Paul, thanking them, says something surprising about needing it.
screen: `I CAN DO ALL THINGS: ON A GYM SHIRT.` → `READ IN PLACE: A THANK-YOU NOTE.` → `A GIFT SENT TO A PRISONER.`

segments.voice: He's glad of the gift, but he doesn't want them to think he was desperate: "Not as it were for want. For I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, to be content therewith." Then he names the states. He knows how to be brought low and how to abound; to be full and to be hungry; to have plenty and to go without. And he says he's been instructed in all of it. The Greek word is the one used for being initiated into a secret. Paul has learned the secret of being content. Then: "I can do all things in him who strengtheneth me." All things, here, means both: hunger and plenty, prison and freedom. Not winning, but standing steady through either. The word for content is autarkēs, and it's borrowed. It was an ideal the Stoic and Cynic philosophers prized: self-sufficient, needing nothing outside yourself. Paul takes their word and changes its center. Not sufficient in myself, but sufficient in him. And notice the first verb: I have learned. Contentment, for Paul, isn't a personality type. It's a skill, and it took practice, and he learned it in some very hard places. Catholic teaching on the tenth commandment speaks of the same freedom: a heart that isn't ruled by envy or by the need for more, which the Catechism calls poverty of heart. And Paul doesn't despise the gift either. He calls it a sweet fragrance, a sacrifice pleasing to God. Content doesn't mean ungrateful. It means grateful, without being owned.

Don't name what's missing; let what's here be enough, and if a want shows up, let it pass by. If you pray, say today's verse slowly; if not, simply rest in what's already here.

592.title: Put on mercy (Colossians 3:12–17)
592.hook: put on mercy, kindness, humility, and above all charity
592.howItsDone: Traditionally, a priest says a short vesting prayer as he puts on each vestment before Mass; the prayers are optional today but still used by some, and many Catholics pray a morning offering at the start of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a thank-you note from prison: I have learned to be content. Your line was I have learned.

Some clothes change how you stand. A uniform on the first day of a job. A borrowed suit at a funeral. The jersey of your team on game day. Paul writes to Colossae, a small town in what's now Turkey, to a church he seems never to have visited. And in the third chapter he talks about getting dressed. First, take off the old self like a worn-out coat: anger, malice, lying. Then, he says, here is what to put on.
screen: `CLOTHES THAT CHANGE HOW YOU STAND.` → `A CHURCH PAUL NEVER VISITED.` → `TAKE OFF THE OLD, PUT ON THE NEW.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "Put ye on therefore, as the elect of God, holy, and beloved, the bowels of mercy, benignity, humility, modesty, patience." Bowels of mercy sounds strange, but it's honest about the body. The Greek word means the inner organs, the gut, where people of that time felt compassion. We'd say heart. Then the five garments: mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience. And what they're for: "Bearing with one another, and forgiving one another, if any have a complaint against another: even as the Lord hath forgiven you, so do you also." Paul doesn't pretend there will be no complaints. He assumes there will be, and tells them what to wear when it happens. Then the last piece: "But above all these things have charity, which is the bond of perfection." Bond is the word we met in Ephesians: syndesmos, the binding. A chapter earlier Paul used it for the bands that hold a body together. Charity holds the other virtues together. Without it, they come apart. Then the chapter widens: let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, singing psalms and hymns, and whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks. Catholic priests have an old custom that puts this on the body. For centuries, as a priest put on each vestment before Mass, he said a short prayer for a matching virtue: purity with the cincture tied at the waist, for one. The prayers are now optional, but some priests still say them.
screen: `BOWELS OF MERCY: FELT IN THE GUT.` · `FIVE GARMENTS.` · `FOR WHEN THERE'S A COMPLAINT.` · `CHARITY: THE BOND THAT HOLDS IT ALL.` · then, large: `ABOVE ALL THESE THINGS HAVE CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Think of the person most likely to bring you a complaint today, or to get one from you. Of the five, mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness or patience, choose the one you'd most need with them, and give that word to the last thing you'll put on before you go out. If you pray, say Paul's line as you touch it, above all these things have charity; if not, let the cloth carry the word.

Your line: above all, charity. The bond that keeps the rest from coming apart. Day five hundred ninety-two, in the books.

593.title: Pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18)
593.hook: always rejoice, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all things
593.carry: a thread that runs through the whole day
593.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Liturgy of the Hours at set times of day, and some pray the Angelus, traditionally at six, noon and six; Catholics also use short repeated prayers, sometimes called aspirations, throughout the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, syndesmos: mercy, kindness, patience, and above all charity, the bond of perfection. Your line was above all, charity.

Paul had barely started a church in Thessalonica, a port city in northern Greece, when trouble broke out and the believers sent him away by night. He tried to go back and couldn't. So he wrote to a young church he was worried about. Today begins a new stretch, from Thessalonians to Philemon. And near the end of this first letter, Paul packs a whole way of life into three short commands.
screen: `SENT AWAY BY NIGHT.` → `HE COULDN'T GO BACK.` → `THREE SHORT COMMANDS.`

segments.voice: "Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In all things give thanks; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you all." Three words in the middle. Pray without ceasing. How could anyone do that? You have to sleep, cook, answer emails. Christians have given several answers. Saint Augustine said the desire of the heart is itself a prayer: if your longing for God never stops, your prayer never stops, even while your lips are busy with something else. Eastern Christians developed the Jesus Prayer, a short line repeated with the breath until it runs underneath everything. An old Russian book, The Way of a Pilgrim, tells of a man who hears this very verse read in church and sets out walking to learn how to do it. The Catholic Church's answer includes the Liturgy of the Hours: psalms and prayers at set times, morning, evening and night, so that, as the Church sees it, the whole day is offered to God. The Angelus bell, rung in some places morning, noon and evening, does the same thing for anyone within earshot. Now look at the third command. In all things give thanks. In, not for. Paul isn't asking anyone to be grateful for cancer or for prison. He's saying there's something to give thanks for even inside a hard thing. He'd know. He was run out of Thessalonica, and he still opens this letter saying he gives thanks for them always. Pray without ceasing, then, isn't nonstop talking. It's a thread that runs through the whole day.
screen: `HOW COULD ANYONE PRAY WITHOUT CEASING?` · `AUGUSTINE: DESIRE IS PRAYER.` · `THE HOURS, THE ANGELUS.` · `IN ALL THINGS, NOT FOR ALL THINGS.` · then, large: `PRAY WITHOUT CEASING.`

segments.voice: Choose a short line to carry: if you pray, the Jesus Prayer, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner, or Paul's three words; if not, a plain word, like thanks. Say it silently as you breathe in, and again as you breathe out. When your mind wanders, come back without scolding yourself, and let it run underneath, the way the pilgrim learned to.
Adialeiptos, without interval. Paul's command to the Thessalonians: not nonstop words, but a thread of prayer running through the whole day. Today's word.

594.title: Not as others without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18)
594.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the dead, especially in November and on All Souls' Day (November 2), have Masses offered for them, and 1 Thessalonians 4 is among the readings for Catholic funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, adialeiptos: pray without ceasing, and give thanks in all things. Your line was a thread that runs through the whole day.
screen: `A THREAD THAT RUNS THROUGH THE WHOLE DAY.`

segments.voice: The new church in Thessalonica had a fear nobody had prepared them for. They were expecting Jesus to come back soon, maybe within their lifetimes. And then some of their own people died. A father. A friend. Had those who died missed it? Were they simply gone? You can hear those questions behind Paul's answer, written for people standing at a grave. It can still be read at a Catholic funeral.
screen: `WAITING FOR HIS RETURN.` → `THEN SOME OF THEM DIED.` → `HAD THEY MISSED IT?`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "And we will not have you ignorant, brethren, concerning them that are asleep, that you be not sorrowful, even as others who have no hope." Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say don't grieve. He says don't grieve as those without hope. Grief stays. It's the hope that changes it. And notice the word he uses: asleep. It's a gentle word for the dead, and a hopeful one: in Paul's picture, sleep is something you wake from. Then Paul gives the reason for the hope: if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, God will bring with him those who have slept. The dead in Christ won't miss anything. In Paul's picture, they rise first, and the living meet them, and then: "so shall we be always with the Lord." And then the practical instruction: "Wherefore, comfort ye one another with these words." This passage isn't a timetable. It's comfort, meant to be said out loud to someone who's grieving. Catholics put it into practice in many ways. At a funeral, the coffin may be covered with a white pall, recalling the white garment of baptism, and the Easter candle stands beside it. In November the Church prays for the dead, especially on All Souls' Day. And the Latin preface for funerals says it in four words: vita mutatur, non tollitur. Life is changed, not taken away. Christians grieve. They cry at gravesides like anyone. For Paul, the grave is not the end of the story.
screen: `NOT 'DON'T GRIEVE': GRIEVE WITH HOPE.` · `ASLEEP: SOMETHING YOU WAKE FROM.` · `ALWAYS WITH THE LORD.` · `COMFORT ONE ANOTHER.` · then, large: `NOT SORROWFUL, EVEN AS OTHERS WHO HAVE NO HOPE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you've lost; if that's too fresh or too heavy today, choose someone further back, or simply someone the world has lost. Picture their face, let yourself miss them, then remember one good thing about them that you still carry. If you pray, pray for them by name, as Catholics do for their dead; if not, simply hold them, and say their name once, quietly.
Koimaomai, to fall asleep. Paul's word for the Thessalonian dead: asleep, since sleep is something you wake from. Today's word.
Your line: grieve with hope. Grief stays, and the hope changes it. Go gently, and see you tomorrow.

595.title: Stir up the gift (2 Timothy 1:6)
595.hook: Paul tells Timothy to stir up the grace given by the laying on of hands
595.howItsDone: In the Catholic rite of ordination, the bishop silently lays his hands on the head of each candidate and then prays the prayer of consecration; Catholics also speak of stirring up the graces of baptism and confirmation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, koimaomai: the dead asleep, and grief that keeps its hope. Your line was grieve with hope.

In a house warmed by an open hearth, the fire was banked at night: ash raked over the last coals, and left. By morning the hearth looked dead. But brush back the ash, blow gently, add a little kindling, and the flame came back. Paul uses that picture in a letter to Timothy, his young friend and co-worker. The letter says Paul is writing in chains, and that the time of his own departure is near.
screen: `A HEARTH BANKED FOR THE NIGHT.` → `BLOW ON THE COALS.` → `A LETTER TO A YOUNG FRIEND.`

segments.voice: He starts with family. He remembers Timothy's faith, which lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. Faith passed down a kitchen table, two generations deep. Then: "For which cause I admonish thee, that thou stir up the grace of God which is in thee, by the imposition of my hands." Stir up translates one Greek verb, anazōpyrein: to rekindle, to fan back into flame. Paul isn't telling Timothy to get a new gift. He already has it. He's telling him not to let it sit under the ash. Then the next line: "For God hath not given us the spirit of fear: but of power, and of love, and of sobriety." Sobriety here means a sound mind, self-control. Paul's next words suggest Timothy was timid, and that fear is what banks a fire. Catholics read the imposition of hands as the sign of ordination. In the sacrament of holy orders, the bishop lays his hands on the head of the one being ordained, in silence, and prays the prayer of consecration. The Church teaches that ordination marks a person permanently: the gift isn't lost. But it can be neglected, and so can every gift. Catholics speak the same way about the graces of baptism and confirmation. They were given once, but they need breath. Notice the order: given by God, then stirred up by the person. Paul expects Timothy to do the blowing. Grace isn't a fire you light alone. But it's also not a fire that tends itself.
screen: `LOIS, EUNICE, TIMOTHY.` · `REKINDLE: FAN BACK INTO FLAME.` · `NOT THE SPIRIT OF FEAR.` · `THE LAYING ON OF HANDS.` · then, large: `STIR UP THE GRACE OF GOD WHICH IS IN THEE.`

segments.voice: Think of one gift that's gone quiet under the ash: a way you used to pray, a skill you stopped using, a patience or courage you once had. Picture it as a coal, still warm, and picture blowing on it gently: what's one small piece of kindling, ten minutes, a call, a page? If you pray, ask for help to stir it up; if not, simply choose the kindling.
Anazopyrein, to rekindle. Paul's word to Timothy: fan back into flame the grace given by the laying on of hands. Today's word.
Your line: fanned back into flame. And that's week eighty-five: rejoice always, arete, content, syndesmos, adialeiptos, koimaomai, and anazopyrein. Day five hundred ninety-five, done.

chat.says: My confirmation feels like ages ago. Is that grace just gone now?
options: Not gone: like coals under ash, a gift once given can be stirred up and fanned again.
Yes: grace lasts only until your first serious doubt, and then it's gone.
It's gone, unless the bishop who confirmed you lays hands on you again.
chat.meaning: Paul tells Timothy to stir up the grace already in him. Given by God, then fanned by the person: grace isn't a fire that tends itself.
